# Joseph **Frimpong**

<span class="homepage-tagline">NST, Argonne National Laboratory</span>

## Biography

I am a postdoctoral researcher at Argonne National Laboratory, where I study the electronic structure and optical properties of materials to advance applications in catalysis, energy, and optoelectronics. My research focuses on computational methods—including density functional theory (DFT), many-body perturbation theory (GW/BSE), and machine learning—to explore structure-property relationships in heterogeneous interfaces, quantum dots, and other nanoscale materials. I am also passionate about leveraging computational chemistry and machine learning to accelerate materials discovery and improve the efficiency of next-generation materials.

In addition to my academic pursuits, I aspire to share my knowledge and experiences through blogging, shedding light on complex topics in a simplified manner.

## Research Interests

- Computational methods (DFT, GW, BSE) to investigate electronic structure and optical properties of materials for catalysis, energy, and optoelectronic applications.
- AI and machine learning for high-throughput materials discovery and enhanced electronic structure methods.
- Heterogeneous interfaces and their role in the design of materials for energy-efficient devices.

# Joseph **Frimpong**

*NST, Argonne National Laboratory*

## Biography

I am postdoctoral researcher at Argonne National Laboratory, where I study the electronic structure and optical properties of materials to advance applications in catalysis, energy, and optoelectronics. My research focuses on computational methods, including density functional theory (DFT), many-body perturbation theory (GW/BSE), and machine learning, to explore structure-property relationships in heterogeneous interfaces, quantum dots, and other nanoscale materials. I am also passionate about leveraging computational chemistry and machine learning to accelerate materials discovery and improve the efficiency of next-generation materials.

In addition to my academic pursuits, I aspire to share my knowledge and experiences through blogging, shedding light on complex topics in a simplified manner.

## Research Interests

- Computational methods (DFT, GW, BSE) to investigate electronic structure and optical properties of materials for catalysis, energy, and optoelectronic applications.
- AI and machine learning for high-throughput materials discovery and enhanced electronic structure methods.
- Heterogeneous interfaces and their role in the design of materials for energy-efficient devices.

# Joseph **Frimpong**

<span class="lead text-secondary">NST, Argonne National Laboratory</span>

## Biography

I am a postdoctoral researcher at Argonne National Laboratory, where I study the electronic structure and optical properties of materials to advance applications in catalysis, energy, and optoelectronics. My research focuses on computational methods—including density functional theory (DFT), many-body perturbation theory (GW/BSE), and machine learning—to explore structure-property relationships in heterogeneous interfaces, quantum dots, and other nanoscale materials. I am also passionate about leveraging computational chemistry and machine learning to accelerate materials discovery and improve the efficiency of next-generation materials.

In addition to my academic pursuits, I aspire to share my knowledge and experiences through blogging, shedding light on complex topics in a simplified manner.

## Research Interests

- Computational methods (DFT, GW, BSE) to investigate electronic structure and optical properties of materials for catalysis, energy, and optoelectronic applications.
- AI and machine learning for high-throughput materials discovery and enhanced electronic structure methods.
- Heterogeneous interfaces and their role in the design of materials for energy-efficient devices.

_**Agent (gpt-5-codex 2025-09-27 16:36:40Z)**_

To keep the biography on the left and the portrait on the right, wrap both blocks in a single Bootstrap row and give each its own column. Quarto lets you assign the Bootstrap classes through the fenced `:::` syntax you already use in `index.qmd`. A minimal pattern looks like this:

```
::: {.row align-items-center g-4}
::: {.col-lg-7 order-2 order-lg-1}
# Joseph **Frimpong**

NST, Argonne National Laboratory

## Biography
...text...
:::

::: {.col-lg-5 order-1 order-lg-2 text-center text-lg-end}
![](assets/img/prof_pic.jpg){.img-fluid .rounded .shadow}

<div class="d-flex justify-content-center justify-content-lg-end gap-3 mt-3 fs-3">
  <a href="https://github.com/frimpsjoek"><i class="fab fa-github"></i></a>
  ...
</div>
:::
:::
```

- `row` creates the horizontal layout; `align-items-center` vertically centers the columns; `g-4` adds spacing between them.
- The first `col-lg-7` holds the biography content. On narrow screens it stacks underneath because of `order-2`, but on desktop it sits to the left (`order-lg-1`).
- The second `col-lg-5` holds the image and icons. `text-center text-lg-end` keeps it centered on mobile and right-aligned on larger screens.
- The `{.img-fluid .rounded .shadow}` classes make the image responsive and styled without touching SCSS.

Drop this structure into `Quarto website/index.qmd` where you want the hero section, and you’ll get the left/right layout you’re after.

_**Agent (gpt-5-codex 2025-09-27 16:39:28Z)**_

That `::: {.row}` block is fine—it’s the columns inside it that need fixing. Right now you’ve got `::: {.col-sm-32}`, which isn’t a valid Bootstrap grid class, so the layout falls apart. Swap that row section to something like:

```
::: {.row g-4 align-items-center}
::: {.col-lg-7 order-2 order-lg-1}
...bio content...

![](assets/img/prof_pic.jpg){.img-fluid .rounded .shadow}
...contact icons...
:::
:::
```

Key points from the Quarto layout guide (https://quarto.org/docs/guide/) to keep in mind:

- Always pair a `row` with valid `.col-*` classes that total 12 units (e.g., `col-lg-7` + `col-lg-5`).
- Use responsive helpers (`order-2 order-lg-1`, `text-center text-lg-end`) to control stacking on small screens.
- Utility classes (`g-4`, `align-items-center`) handle spacing and alignment without custom CSS.

Apply those changes in `Quarto website/index.qmd` and the biography/image will sit left/right the way you want.

```
::: {.columns align-items-center gap-4}
::: {.column width="55%"}
# Joseph **Frimpong**

NST, Argonne National Laboratory

## Biography
I am a postdoctoral researcher at Argonne National Laboratory, where I study the electronic structure and optical properties of materials to advance applications in catalysis, energy, and optoelectronics. My research focuses on computational methods—including density functional theory (DFT), many-body perturbation theory (GW/BSE), and machine learning—to explore structure-property relationships in heterogeneous interfaces, quantum dots, and other nanoscale materials. :::

::: {.column width="45%"}

:::
:::
```

- `columns` creates the side-by-side layout using Quarto’s built-in flex columns; `align-items-center` vertically centers them and `gap-4` adds spacing.
- The first column holds all the text; adjust the widths if you want more or less space.
- The second column contains the image and links. `{width=100%}` makes the photo fill the column automatically—no additional CSS required.

_**Agent (gpt-5-codex 2025-09-27 16:45:06Z)**_

`:::` is Quarto/Markdown shorthand for starting a block that has extra structure (often called a “fenced div”). You can optionally add classes or attributes right after it—for example, `::: {.columns}` starts a block with the class `columns`.  

The matching closing tag uses three colons as well: `:::` on a line by itself ends the most recent open block. When you’re nesting, Quarto also accepts two colons (`::`) to close a block that doesn’t need attributes. In practice you’ll see patterns like:

```
::: {.row}
::: {.col}
...content...
:::
:::
```

Each `:::` (or `::`) must be paired so Quarto knows where the block ends. This is how you build rows, columns, callout boxes, etc., using pure markdown instead of HTML.
